title: Time and Work
subtitle: Quantitative Aptitude – Placement Preparation
description: Learn work-rate concepts, efficiency methods, combined work, wages, worker-based problems, alternate-day work and pipes and cisterns.
learningObjectives: Understand the relationship between work, rate and time.
Calculate one-day work and work efficiency.
Find the time taken by two or more people working together.
Compare the efficiencies of different workers.
Use the LCM method to solve Time and Work problems quickly.
Solve problems in which workers join or leave a task.
Calculate wages according to work completed.
Solve problems involving men, women, machines, days and working hours.
Apply Time and Work concepts to pipes and cisterns.
Use placement-test shortcuts to solve questions efficiently.

sections.heading: 1. Basic Concept of Time and Work
content: Time and Work problems study the relationship between the amount of work completed, the rate of working and the time taken.
A person who works faster completes more work in the same amount of time.
For a fixed amount of work, efficiency and time are inversely proportional.
If efficiency increases, the time required decreases.
formulas: Work done = Rate of work × Time
Rate of work = Work done / Time
Time = Work done / Rate of work
Efficiency ∝ 1 / Time

examples.question: A worker completes 40 units of work in 5 days. Find the worker's daily rate.
examples.solution: Daily rate = 40/5 = 8 units per day.

examples.question: A machine produces 15 units per hour. How many units will it produce in 8 hours?
examples.solution: Work done = Rate × Time = 15 × 8 = 120 units.

sections.heading: 2. One-Day Work
content: If a person completes an entire piece of work in a certain number of days, the person's one-day work is the reciprocal of the number of days.
One-day work represents the fraction of the total work completed in one day.
Once one-day work is known, the work completed in any number of days can be calculated.
formulas: If A completes a work in x days, A's one-day work = 1/x
Work completed in n days = n/x
Time required = 1 / One-day work

examples.question: A can complete a work in 12 days. Find A's one-day work.
examples.solution: A's one-day work = 1/12.

examples.question: A completes a work in 15 days. What fraction of the work will A complete in 5 days?
examples.solution: Work completed in 5 days = 5/15 = 1/3.

examples.question: A worker completes 1/18 of a task per day. How many days will the worker take to complete the task?

sections.heading: 3. Combined Work of Two People
content: When two people work together, their individual rates are added.
The combined rate represents the fraction of work completed by both people in one day.
The reciprocal of the combined one-day work gives the total time required.
formulas: Combined one-day work = 1/x + 1/y
Time taken together = xy / (x + y)
Here, x and y are the individual times taken by A and B.

examples.question: A can complete a work in 12 days and B can complete it in 18 days. Find the time taken when they work together.
examples.solution: Combined work per day = 1/12 + 1/18 = 3/36 + 2/36 = 5/36. Time = 36/5 = 7.2 days.

examples.question: A completes a task in 10 days and B completes it in 15 days. How long will they take together?

sections.heading: 4. Combined Work of Three People
content: When three people work together, add the one-day work of all three people.
The same method can be extended to any number of workers.
After adding their work rates, take the reciprocal to find the required time.
formulas: Combined one-day work = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z
Time taken together = 1 / Combined one-day work

examples.question: A, B and C can complete a work individually in 12, 18 and 36 days. Find the time taken when all three work together.
examples.solution: Combined work = 1/12 + 1/18 + 1/36 = 3/36 + 2/36 + 1/36 = 6/36 = 1/6. Therefore, they complete the work in 6 days.

examples.question: A, B and C can complete a task in 8, 12 and 24 days respectively. Find their combined time.
examples.solution: Combined work = 1/8 + 1/12 + 1/24 = 3/24 + 2/24 + 1/24 = 6/24 = 1/4. Therefore, the work is completed in 4 days.

sections.heading: 5. LCM Method
content: The LCM method avoids complicated fractions.
Take the least common multiple of the given completion times as the total number of work units.
Divide the total work units by each worker's time to obtain the worker's daily efficiency.
Add the efficiencies of workers who work together.
formulas: Total work = LCM of individual completion times
Efficiency = Total work / Number of days
Time taken together = Total work / Combined efficiency

examples.question: A completes a work in 12 days and B completes it in 18 days. Solve using the LCM method.
examples.solution: LCM of 12 and 18 = 36 units. A's efficiency = 36/12 = 3 units per day. B's efficiency = 36/18 = 2 units per day. Combined efficiency = 5 units per day. Time = 36/5 = 7.2 days.

examples.question: A, B and C complete a work in 10, 15 and 30 days respectively. Find their combined time using work units.
examples.solution: LCM = 30 units. Efficiencies are 3, 2 and 1 units per day. Combined efficiency = 6 units per day. Time = 30/6 = 5 days.

sections.heading: 6. Efficiency and Time
content: Efficiency represents the amount of work completed in one unit of time.
A more efficient worker completes the same work in less time.
For the same amount of work, efficiency and time are inversely proportional.
If the efficiency ratio is known, reverse the ratio to obtain the time ratio.
formulas: Efficiency ratio = Inverse of time ratio
If efficiency of A : B = m : n, then time taken by A : B = n : m
If time taken by A : B = m : n, then efficiency of A : B = n : m

examples.question: The efficiency ratio of A and B is 3:2. Find the ratio of the times taken by them.
examples.solution: Time ratio is the inverse of efficiency ratio. Therefore, time taken by A : B = 2:3.

examples.question: A takes 12 days and B takes 18 days to complete the same work. Find their efficiency ratio.
examples.solution: Efficiency ratio A:B = 18:12 = 3:2.

examples.question: A is twice as efficient as B. If B completes a work in 20 days, find the time taken by A.
examples.solution: A's efficiency is twice B's efficiency, so A takes half the time. Time taken by A = 20/2 = 10 days.

sections.heading: 7. Finding Individual Time from Combined Time
content: Sometimes the combined completion time and one person's individual time are given.
Subtract the known person's one-day work from the combined one-day work.
The remaining rate belongs to the other worker.
formulas: B's one-day work = Combined one-day work − A's one-day work
If A and B together take T days and A alone takes x days, B alone takes xT / (x − T) days

examples.question: A and B together complete a task in 8 days. A alone completes it in 12 days. Find the time taken by B alone.
examples.solution: B's work = 1/8 − 1/12 = 3/24 − 2/24 = 1/24. Therefore, B takes 24 days.

examples.question: A and B together take 6 days. A alone takes 10 days. Find B's individual time.

sections.heading: 8. Work Completed and Remaining Work
content: When workers work for only part of the total time, first calculate the amount of work they complete.
Subtract the completed work from the total work to find the remaining work.
The remaining time depends on the rate of the worker or group that continues.
formulas: Work completed = Rate × Number of days
Remaining work = Total work − Completed work
Time for remaining work = Remaining work / Remaining rate

examples.question: A can complete a work in 20 days. How much work remains after A works for 8 days?
examples.solution: Work completed = 8/20 = 2/5. Remaining work = 1 − 2/5 = 3/5.

examples.question: A and B together can complete a work in 10 days. They work together for 4 days. What fraction of the work remains?
examples.solution: Work completed = 4/10 = 2/5. Remaining work = 1 − 2/5 = 3/5.

sections.heading: 9. Workers Joining or Leaving
content: Some questions involve one worker beginning the task and another worker joining later.
Other questions involve workers leaving before the task is completed.
Divide the work into separate stages according to the workers present during each stage.
Calculate the work completed in each stage before finding the remaining work.
formulas: Stage work = Combined rate during the stage × Duration of the stage
Total completed work = Sum of work completed in all stages
Remaining time = Remaining work / Current combined rate

examples.question: A can complete a work in 12 days and B in 18 days. A works alone for 4 days, after which B joins. Find the total time required.
examples.solution: A completes 4/12 = 1/3 of the work. Remaining work = 2/3. Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36. Time for remaining work = (2/3) ÷ (5/36) = (2/3) × (36/5) = 24/5 = 4.8 days. Total time = 4 + 4.8 = 8.8 days.

examples.question: A and B can complete a work in 10 days. They work together for 6 days, and then B leaves. A completes the remaining work in 8 days. Find A's individual completion time.
examples.solution: Together they complete 6/10 = 3/5 of the work. Remaining work = 2/5. A completes 2/5 in 8 days, so A's daily work = (2/5)/8 = 1/20. Therefore, A alone takes 20 days.

sections.heading: 10. Alternate-Day Work
content: In alternate-day problems, workers perform the task on different days.
Calculate the work completed during one complete cycle.
A two-day cycle usually consists of one day of A's work and one day of B's work.
Continue counting complete cycles and then calculate the work done on the final day.
formulas: Work in one two-day cycle = A's one-day work + B's one-day work
Number of complete cycles = Work completed before the final partial cycle / Work per cycle

examples.question: A can complete a work in 10 days and B in 15 days. They work on alternate days beginning with A. Find the work completed in two days.
examples.solution: Work completed in two days = 1/10 + 1/15 = 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6.

examples.question: A can complete a task in 4 days and B in 12 days. They work on alternate days beginning with A. Find the total time required.
examples.solution: In two days, work completed = 1/4 + 1/12 = 1/3. In 6 days, three cycles complete the entire work. Therefore, total time = 6 days.

sections.heading: 11. Men, Days and Work
content: For workers with equal efficiency, the total work is proportional to the number of workers multiplied by the number of days.
More workers require fewer days to complete the same task.
Fewer workers require more days when all other conditions remain unchanged.
formulas: Work ∝ Number of workers × Number of days
Required days = (Original workers × Original days) / New workers

examples.question: 12 workers complete a task in 15 days. How many days will 20 workers take?
examples.solution: 12 × 15 = 20 × D. Therefore, D = 180/20 = 9 days.

examples.question: 18 workers complete a task in 24 days. How many workers are needed to complete it in 16 days?
examples.solution: 18 × 24 = M × 16. Therefore, M = 432/16 = 27 workers.

sections.heading: 12. Men, Days and Working Hours
content: When daily working hours change, include hours in the work relationship.
The total work is proportional to the number of workers, number of days and working hours per day.
This method assumes that all workers have equal efficiency.
formulas: Work ∝ Workers × Days × Hours per day

examples.question: 10 workers working 6 hours per day complete a task in 15 days. How many days will 15 workers working 8 hours per day take?
20 workers working 8 hours per day complete a task in 12 days. How many workers working 6 hours per day are required to complete it in 16 days?
examples.solution: 20 × 12 × 8 = M × 16 × 6. Therefore, M = 1920/96 = 20 workers.

sections.heading: 13. Different Categories of Workers
content: Men, women, children or machines may have different efficiencies.
Convert one category into an equivalent number of another category using the given efficiency ratio.
After conversion, apply the standard workers-and-days relationship.
formulas: Equivalent workers = Number of workers × Relative efficiency
Total work = Workers × Efficiency × Time
If m men are equivalent to w women, then efficiency of one man : one woman = w : m

examples.question: 3 men can complete the same work as 5 women. Find the efficiency ratio of one man to one woman.
examples.solution: 3 men = 5 women. Therefore, efficiency of one man : one woman = 5:3.

examples.question: 2 machines can produce the same output as 5 workers. How many workers are equivalent to 6 machines?
examples.solution: 1 machine = 5/2 workers. Therefore, 6 machines = 6 × 5/2 = 15 workers.

sections.heading: 14. Work and Wages
content: Wages are generally divided according to the amount of work completed.
When workers work for the same amount of time, wages are divided according to their efficiency ratio.
When workers work for different durations, wages are divided according to efficiency multiplied by time.
formulas: Wage ratio = Work-done ratio
Work done = Efficiency × Time
Wage ratio = Efficiency ratio × Time ratio

examples.question: A and B complete a job together and their efficiency ratio is 3:2. If they receive $500, find their individual shares.
A and B have efficiencies in the ratio 2:3. A works for 6 days and B works for 4 days. Find their wage ratio.
examples.solution: A's work : B's work = 2 × 6 : 3 × 4 = 12:12 = 1:1. Therefore, wages are divided equally.

sections.heading: 15. Work Completed in a Given Number of Days
content: When a worker's total completion time is known, multiply the one-day work by the number of days worked.
The same approach can be used for a group of workers.
Make sure that the work completed does not exceed the total work.
formulas: Individual work in d days = d/x
Combined work in d days = d × Combined one-day work

examples.question: A completes a task in 16 days. What percentage of the task is completed in 4 days?
examples.solution: Work completed = 4/16 = 1/4. Percentage completed = 25%.

examples.question: A and B can complete a task in 12 and 18 days. What fraction do they complete together in 3 days?
examples.solution: Combined daily work = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36. Work in 3 days = 3 × 5/36 = 15/36 = 5/12.

sections.heading: 16. Finding Efficiency from Percentage Comparison
content: Efficiency may be compared using percentages.
If A is a certain percentage more efficient than B, assign B an efficiency of 100 units.
Increase or decrease the efficiency according to the given percentage.
Reverse the efficiency ratio to find the time ratio.
formulas: If A is p% more efficient than B, efficiency ratio A:B = (100 + p):100
If A is p% less efficient than B, efficiency ratio A:B = (100 − p):100
Time ratio = Inverse of efficiency ratio

examples.question: A is 25% more efficient than B. Find the efficiency and time ratios.
examples.solution: Let B's efficiency be 100. A's efficiency = 125. Efficiency ratio A:B = 125:100 = 5:4. Time ratio A:B = 4:5.

examples.question: A is 20% less efficient than B. If B completes a work in 16 days, find A's time.
examples.solution: Efficiency ratio A:B = 80:100 = 4:5. Time ratio A:B = 5:4. A's time = 16 × 5/4 = 20 days.

sections.heading: 17. Pipes and Cisterns – Basic Concepts
content: Pipes and cisterns use the same principles as Time and Work.
A filling pipe performs positive work because it adds water to the tank.
An emptying pipe or leak performs negative work because it removes water.
The capacity of the tank is treated as the total work.
formulas: If a pipe fills a tank in x hours, filling rate = 1/x
If a pipe empties a tank in y hours, emptying rate = −1/y
Net rate = Sum of filling rates − Sum of emptying rates
Required time = 1 / Net rate

examples.question: A pipe fills a tank in 12 hours. What fraction of the tank does it fill in one hour?
examples.solution: One-hour filling rate = 1/12.

examples.question: An outlet empties a tank in 15 hours. What is its one-hour rate?
examples.solution: Since it removes water, its rate is −1/15.

sections.heading: 18. Two Filling Pipes
content: When two inlet pipes are opened together, add their filling rates.
The combined filling time is found in the same way as the combined work of two people.
formulas: Combined rate = 1/x + 1/y
Combined filling time = xy / (x + y)

examples.question: Pipe A fills a tank in 10 hours and Pipe B fills it in 15 hours. Find the time taken when both are opened together.
Two pipes fill a tank in 12 hours and 18 hours. Find their combined filling time.
examples.solution: Combined rate = 1/12 + 1/18 = 5/36. Time = 36/5 = 7.2 hours.

sections.heading: 19. Inlet Pipe and Outlet Pipe
content: When a filling pipe and an emptying pipe are opened together, subtract the emptying rate from the filling rate.
The tank fills only when the filling rate is greater than the emptying rate.
The tank empties when the emptying rate is greater than the filling rate.
formulas: Net filling rate = 1/x − 1/y
If y > x, net filling time = xy / (y − x)
Here, x is filling time and y is emptying time.

examples.question: A pipe fills a tank in 8 hours and a leak empties it in 24 hours. Find the time taken to fill the tank when both operate.
examples.solution: Net rate = 1/8 − 1/24 = 3/24 − 1/24 = 2/24 = 1/12. Therefore, the tank fills in 12 hours.

examples.question: An inlet fills a tank in 12 hours and an outlet empties it in 18 hours. Find the net filling time.
examples.solution: Net rate = 1/12 − 1/18 = 3/36 − 2/36 = 1/36. Therefore, the tank fills in 36 hours.

sections.heading: 20. Leak Detected after Filling Begins
content: A leak reduces the effective filling rate of a pipe.
If the normal filling time and the actual filling time are given, subtract the actual net rate from the inlet rate to find the leak rate.
Take the reciprocal of the leak rate to find the time in which the leak alone would empty the tank.
formulas: Leak rate = Inlet rate − Actual net rate
Leak rate = 1/x − 1/y
Leak emptying time = 1 / Leak rate

examples.question: A pipe normally fills a tank in 6 hours, but because of a leak it takes 9 hours. In how many hours can the leak empty the full tank?
examples.solution: Leak rate = 1/6 − 1/9 = 3/18 − 2/18 = 1/18. Therefore, the leak can empty the tank in 18 hours.

examples.question: A pipe fills a tank in 8 hours, but a leak increases the filling time to 12 hours. Find the leak's emptying time.
examples.solution: Leak rate = 1/8 − 1/12 = 3/24 − 2/24 = 1/24. Therefore, the leak empties the tank in 24 hours.

quickShortcuts.title: One-day work
quickShortcuts.note: If a person completes a task in x days, the person's one-day work is 1/x.

quickShortcuts.title: Combined work
quickShortcuts.note: Add the individual one-day work rates of all people working together.

quickShortcuts.title: Two-worker shortcut
quickShortcuts.note: If A and B take x and y days individually, together they take xy/(x+y) days.

quickShortcuts.title: Use the LCM method
quickShortcuts.note: Take the LCM of the given completion times as total work to avoid fractions.

quickShortcuts.title: Efficiency and time
quickShortcuts.note: Efficiency and time are inversely proportional for the same amount of work.

quickShortcuts.title: Reverse the ratio
quickShortcuts.note: Reverse the efficiency ratio to obtain the time ratio.

quickShortcuts.title: Workers and days
quickShortcuts.note: For equal efficiency and fixed work, workers × days remains constant.

quickShortcuts.title: Include working hours
quickShortcuts.note: When hours change, use workers × days × hours.

quickShortcuts.title: Workers joining later
quickShortcuts.note: Divide the work into stages and calculate completed and remaining work separately.

quickShortcuts.title: Alternate-day work
quickShortcuts.note: Find the work completed in one complete cycle before counting the final day.

quickShortcuts.title: Wage distribution
quickShortcuts.note: Divide wages in the ratio of the actual work completed.

quickShortcuts.title: Filling pipes
quickShortcuts.note: Treat filling pipes as positive work rates.

quickShortcuts.title: Outlet or leak
quickShortcuts.note: Treat an outlet pipe or leak as a negative work rate.

quickShortcuts.title: Net pipe rate
quickShortcuts.note: Add inlet rates and subtract outlet rates.

quickShortcuts.title: Check the answer
quickShortcuts.note: People working together must normally take less time than either person working alone.

commonMistakes: Adding the number of days instead of adding work rates.
Forgetting that efficiency and time are inversely proportional.
Using the efficiency ratio directly as the time ratio.
Failing to calculate the work completed before a worker joins or leaves.
Using the total work instead of the remaining work in the final stage.
Ignoring the order of workers in alternate-day problems.
Forgetting to include working hours when daily hours change.
Assuming men, women and machines have equal efficiency without conversion.
Dividing wages according to time instead of actual work completed.
Treating an outlet pipe as a positive rate.
Adding filling and emptying rates instead of subtracting them.
Forgetting that a leak increases the total filling time.
Using inconsistent time units such as days and hours in the same calculation.
Rounding intermediate fractional values too early.
